<problem>
Let \(n\) be an integer that is either even with \(n\ge 10\) or odd with \(n\ge 15\). Let \(\mathcal R_n\) be the class of finite connected simple undirected graphs on \(n\) vertices in which all vertices have the same degree; this common degree may vary between graphs in \(\mathcal R_n\). Here simple means that loops and multiple edges are forbidden.

For \(G\in\mathcal R_n\), let \((X_k)_{k\ge0}\) be the discrete-time random walk that moves at each step to a uniformly chosen neighbor of its current vertex. For \(v\in V(G)\), set
\[
T_v=\inf\{k\ge0:X_k=v\},
\]
and let \(\mathbb E_u\) denote expectation when \(X_0=u\). Define
\[
\tau(G)=\max_{u,v\in V(G)}\bigl(\mathbb E_uT_v+\mathbb E_vT_u\bigr),
\qquad
 t_n=\max_{G\in\mathcal R_n}\tau(G).
\]
Determine an explicit exact formula for \(t_n\) as a function of \(n\) throughout the stated domain.
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer is an explicit exact formula for t_n for every even integer n ≥ 10 and every odd integer n ≥ 15. The formula may be piecewise, but its cases must cover the entire stated domain and specify a unique exact value for each n.

A team of 4 agents was told that the answer is \displaystyle t_n=\begin{cases}\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{596}{115}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv2\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{278}{45}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv4\pmod5.\end{cases} and asked to prove it (told: Proving this formula takes two halves, for every even \(n\ge10\) and every odd \(n\ge15\): every \(G\in\mathcal R_n\) has \(\tau(G)\) at most the stated piecewise value for \(n\), and some \(G\in\mathcal R_n\) has \(\tau(G)\) exactly equal to that value.), writing Python that checks every step. Their run ended: all agents idle, the judge found the proof complete. The answer they were told may be wrong: teams told a wrong answer sometimes stop at bounds or partial results, and sometimes claim a proof anyway. You decide whether this team proved \displaystyle t_n=\begin{cases}\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{596}{115}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv2\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{278}{45}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv4\pmod5.\end{cases}: whether a search for the answer can stop here and report \displaystyle t_n=\begin{cases}\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{596}{115}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv2\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{278}{45}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv4\pmod5.\end{cases} as proved.

Their whole record is in your folder, read-only:
- record/prompt.md: what the team was told.
- record/channel.md: their Slack channel (#proof), every post in order.
- record/finals.md: each agent's last reply, often its write-up.
- record/transcripts/<agent>.md: each agent's whole run: its reasoning summaries, its messages, every file it wrote and ran, and what each run printed.
- workspace/: the folder the team shared, as they left it (code, data, certificates, write-ups).
- agents/<agent>/: each agent's own folder (its scratchpad.py and files).

Your tools: list_files, read_file, grep, write_file (files of your own folder; not inside record/, workspace/ or agents/), and run_python, which runs a Python file of your folder in a sandbox with the team's libraries (NumPy, SciPy, SymPy, mpmath, NetworkX, Sage via passagemath, ...), no network, up to 1200 s a run. A run can read workspace/ and agents/ but not change them: to rerun a team's script that writes files, copy it into your folder and change where it writes. Its working directory is your folder, so `sys.path.insert(0, "workspace")` imports the team's shared code.

Do this:
1. Find what the team claims at the end: a complete proof of \displaystyle t_n=\begin{cases}\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{596}{115}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv2\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{278}{45}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv4\pmod5.\end{cases}, or less (bounds, a partial result, a reduction, a result conditional on something unproved, or no conclusion). Start from record/finals.md and the end of record/channel.md.
2. If they claim a complete proof, reconstruct the final proof and find its decisive steps: those that force \displaystyle t_n=\begin{cases}\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{596}{115}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv2\pmod5,\\[2pt]n^2-\frac{278}{45}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv4\pmod5.\end{cases} rather than another answer. Check each:
   - an argument written out: check it yourself;
   - a computation: read the code and check that it computes what the step needs (the right objects, the right field or precision, nothing assumed that is to be shown); rerun it, or its decisive part, when that is feasible, rather than trusting the reported output;
   - a cited result: whether it is a precise statement whose hypotheses hold here. Your recollection of the literature is no better evidence than the team's: a citation that was questioned in the record and settled only by agents recalling or agreeing is not settled.

- gap: they claim a complete proof, but a substantive step is missing, only asserted, left conditional on an unproved claim, or rests on a computation that doesn't establish what the step needs;
- false: a step of the claimed proof is wrong;

11	```
12	The recorded run took approximately 44 seconds. Instructions are in `README.md`; the command is
13	```bash
14	python RUN_ALL.py
15	```
16	using Python with SageMath, NetworkX, and SymPy available. No floating-point resistance calculations, random searches, external graph generators, or downloads are used.
17	
18	Below is the argument’s organization and the principal calculations. The linked proof includes the detailed cut arguments, all exceptional cases, and the enumeration-exhaustivity proofs.
19	
20	## 1. Reduction to effective resistance
21	
22	Write \(R_G(x,y)\) for effective resistance with unit resistances on the edges. The commute-time identity gives
23	\[
24	\mathbb E_xT_y+\mathbb E_yT_x=2|E(G)|R_G(x,y).
25	\]
26	Consequently, for a \(d\)-regular graph,
27	\[
28	\tau(G)=dn\max_{x,y}R_G(x,y).                                      \tag{1}
29	\]
30	
31	For completeness, if \(h_y(x)=\mathbb E_xT_y\), then
32	\[
33	Lh_y=\deg-2|E(G)|e_y.
34	\]
35	Thus
36	\[
37	L(h_y-h_x)=2|E(G)|(e_x-e_y).
38	\]
39	Taking the potential difference between \(x\) and \(y\) proves the identity.
40	
41	The proof uses Thomson’s principle, the resistance triangle inequality, Foster’s identity
42	\[
43	\sum_{e\in E(G)}R_G(e)=n-1,
44	\]
45	and exact solutions of grounded integer Laplacians.
46	
47	## 2. The sharp cubic bound
48	
49	For every connected cubic graph of even order \(n\ge10\),
50	\[
51	\max_{x,y}R_G(x,y)\le
52	\begin{cases}
53	n/2-9/4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\
54	n/2-11/4,&n\equiv0\pmod4.
55	\end{cases}                                                     \tag{2}
56	\]
57	
58	Here is the bridge-block argument.
59	
60	Delete all bridges. Every nontrivial remaining component is two-vertex-connected: a cut vertex in a bridgeless graph would need degree at least four. Therefore a component of order \(b\) has resistance between any two vertices at most \(b/4\), by sending current along the two arcs of a cycle containing them.
61	
62	Every component separated by one bridge contains at least five vertices. Indeed, its degree sum is \(3b-1\), so \(b\) is odd, and simplicity excludes \(b=1,3\).
63	
64	Fix \(x,y\) and follow their bridge-block path. Assign every off-path branch to the path block where it attaches. For a path block let \(w\) be its assigned order and \(r\) its internal resistance, and put
65	\[
66	D=\frac w2-1-r.
67	\]
68	Series resistance gives
69	\[
70	R_G(x,y)=\frac n2-1-\sum D.
71	\]
72	The following bounds hold:
73	
74	- each terminal block has \(D\ge5/8\);
75	- a terminal block other than the five-vertex standard cap has \(D\ge9/8\);
76	- each internal block has \(D\ge0\);
77	- a nonstandard internal block has \(D\ge1/2\).
78	
79	The only small resistance calculations needed are terminal caps of orders five and seven. Exhaustive exact enumeration gives respectively
80	\[
81	\frac78,\qquad\frac{11}{8}.
82	\]
83	All other cases follow from the cycle bound and the five vertices contributed by every off-path branch.
84	
85	Thus \(\sum D\ge5/4\). If every block is standard, the order is \(10+4k\); hence when \(n\equiv0\pmod4\), some block contributes an additional \(1/2\). This proves (2).
86	
87	Equality is attained by chains consisting of:
88	
89	- two five-vertex caps, or one five-vertex and one seven-vertex cap;
90	- \(k\) copies of \(K_4-e\), whose two degree-two ports have resistance \(1\);
91	- bridges between consecutive ports.
92	
93	Their orders and terminal resistances are
94	\[
95	\begin{array}{c|c}
96	n& R\\ \hline
97	10+4k&2k+11/4\\
98	12+4k&2k+13/4 .
99	\end{array}
100	\]
101	Multiplying by \(3n\) gives the two asserted even formulas.
102	
103	## 3. The sharp four-regular bound
104	
105	The central local estimates concern two-connected graphs with degree-two ports and all other vertices of degree four.
106	
107	For a two-port graph of order \(b\),
108	\[
109	R(s,t)\le\frac{3b+2}{16}.                                        \tag{3}
110	\]
111	For a one-port graph of order \(b\),
112	\[
113	\max_vR(s,v)\le\frac{3b}{16}-\frac{13}{40}.                       \tag{4}
114	\]
115	
116	These are proved by a maximal nested chain of two-edge cuts. Give each interlayer edge current \(1/2\). Maximality and even cut parity imply, for every subset of a layer,
117	\[
118	|\delta_A(U)|\ge |\sigma(U)|+2,
119	\]
120	where \(\sigma\) is the entering-minus-leaving incidence count. Consequently the prescribed boundary currents can be completed internally with edge currents bounded by \(1/4\).
121	
122	The resulting energy estimates prove (3), except for layers of orders four and five; their exact maximum prescribed-current energies are \(1/4\) and \(1/3\). For (4), the terminal-tail calculation reduces to orders six through ten. Their exact maximum internal energies are
123	\[
124	\frac3{10},\quad\frac{73}{180},\quad
125	\frac{37}{70},\quad\frac{59}{90},\quad\frac{21}{20}.
126	\]
127	All these finite checks are recomputed by the certificate.
128	
129	The small one-port and two-port resistance maxima are:
130	
131	\[
132	\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
133	b&6&7&8&9&10&11&12&13\\ \hline
134	\text{one port}&
135	\frac45&\frac{104}{115}&\frac{36}{35}&\frac{52}{45}&
136	\frac{31}{20}&\frac{91}{55}&\frac95&\frac{343}{180}\\[2pt]
137	\text{two ports}&
138	\frac54&\frac43&\frac32&\frac{19}{12}&
139	2&\frac{25}{12}&\frac94&\frac73
140	\end{array}                                                     \tag{5}
141	\]
142	
143	These are exhaustive rational computations, covering **639,086 generated degree-sequence representatives** through order thirteen. The generator’s symmetry pruning is justified in the proof; it does not discard any graph up to relabeling.
144	
145	Define the defects
146	\[
147	\epsilon_b=\frac b4-R_{\rm cap},\qquad
148	\delta_b=\frac{b-1}{4}-R_{\rm middle}.
149	\]
150	By (3)–(4), for \(b\ge14\),
151	\[
152	\epsilon_b\ge\frac65,\qquad \delta_b\ge\frac12.
153	\]
154	These cannot improve the optimum. Orders eleven through thirteen are likewise dominated in their residue classes. Only orders six through ten remain.
155	
156	If the terminal cap orders are \(a,b\) and the middle-block orders are \(b_i\), then
157	\[
158	n=a+b-1+\sum_i(b_i-1)
159	\]
160	and
161	\[
162	R=\frac n4-
163	\left(\epsilon_a+\epsilon_b-\frac14+\sum_i\delta_{b_i}\right).
164	\]
165	Exact min-plus optimization on the five residues gives
166	\[
167	\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
168	n\bmod5&0&1&2&3&4\\ \hline
169	\text{minimum defect}&
170	\frac75&\frac{23}{20}&\frac{149}{115}&\frac75&\frac{139}{90}.
171	\end{array}                                                     \tag{6}
172	\]
173	
174	Branching cannot improve this: an off-path port contributes at least five additional vertices. Its defect is at least \(1\) for an internal block or \(5/4\) for an end block, exceeding every potentially competitive choice.
175	
176	When no articulation separates the two marked vertices, the same cut argument gives
177	\[
178	R(x,y)\le
179	\max\left\{\frac n8,\frac{3n}{16}-\frac{31}{40}\right\},
180	\]
181	which is below all the required odd-order bounds for \(n\ge15\).
182	
183	Therefore every four-regular graph of allowed odd order satisfies
184	\[
185	R_{\max}\le
186	\begin{cases}
187	n/4-7/5,&n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\
188	n/4-23/20,&n\equiv1\pmod5,\\
189	n/4-149/115,&n\equiv2\pmod5,\\
190	n/4-139/90,&n\equiv4\pmod5.
191	\end{cases}                                                     \tag{7}
192	\]
193	Multiplying by \(4n\) produces precisely the four odd formulas.
194	
195	## 4. Why no other degree is larger
196	
197	This is essential: proving only the cubic and four-regular subclasses would not suffice.
198	
199	The complete degree reductions proved in the supplied proof are summarized below. Every entry bounds \(dR_G(x,y)\).
200	
201	\[
202	\begin{array}{c|c|c}
203	n&d&\text{upper bound}\\ \hline
204	\text{either}&2& n/2\\
205	\text{either}&d\ge n/2& n/2\\
206	\text{even}&4&\text{strictly below the cubic target}\\
207	\text{even}&5,6&3n/2-33/4\\
208	\text{even}&d\ge7&
209	\displaystyle
210	\frac{d^2+8d+3}{(d+1)(d+2)}n-d-2+\frac2{d+2}\\[4pt]
211	\text{odd}&6,8&n-278/45\\
212	\text{odd}&d\ge10&
213	\displaystyle
214	\frac{d^2+15d-8}{2(d+1)^2}n
215	-\frac{d^3+4d^2+15d-8}{2(d+1)^2}.
216	\end{array}                                                     \tag{8}
217	\]
218	
219	For odd \(n\), regularity forces \(d\) even, so this list covers every possible degree.
220	
221	Some useful details behind these reductions follow.
222	
223	### Dense graphs
224	
225	For \(d\ge n/2\), the complement Laplacian gives
226	\[
227	\lambda_2(L_G)\ge2d-n+2.
228	\]
229	Thus
230	\[
231	R(x,y)\le\frac2{2d-n+2},
232	\qquad
233	dR(x,y)\le\frac n2.
234	\]
235	A cycle also has commute diameter at most \(n^2/2\). Both are below the stated targets.
236	
237	### Even orders, degrees five and six
238	
239	The proofs use constant-width cut chains—not an assumption that arbitrary changing-width interfaces can be glued.
240	
241	A useful exact flow estimate is this. Suppose a simple acyclic integer flow on \(a\) vertices has edge capacity \(C\) and total positive injection at most \(F\). In a topological ordering,
242	\[
243	\sum_e j_e\,\operatorname{length}(e)\le F(a-1).
244	\]
245	At most \(a-1\) edges have length one, so
246	\[
247	\sum_e j_e^2
248	 \le \frac{C(F+C)(a-1)}2.                                       \tag{9}
249	\]
250	
251	For degree five, maximal chains of cuts of sizes two and three have matching uniform interface currents. Formula (9), the exact small tails in the certificate, and bridge reassembly give
252	\[
253	R(x,y)\le\frac{3n}{10}-\frac{33}{20}.
254	\]
255	
256	For degree six, all cuts are even. If the marked vertices have connectivity at least four, integral quarter-capacity flow gives
257	\[
258	R(x,y)\le\frac{5(n-1)}{32}.
259	\]
260	Otherwise use a maximal two-cut chain. Ordinary layers have order at least seven and charged energy at most one quarter their order. Each terminal tail retains a defect of at least \(11/16\), giving
261	\[
262	R(x,y)\le\frac n4-\frac{11}{8}.
263	\]
264	
265	### Even orders, degrees at least seven
266	
267	Every adjacent edge has resistance at least
268	\[
269	r_0=\frac2{d+1}.
270	\]
271	If its endpoints are not closed-neighborhood twins, a four-vertex Dirichlet test improves this to
272	\[
273	r_1=\frac{2(d+1)}{d(d+2)}.
274	\]
275	There are at least \(3n/2\) nontwin edges for \(d\ge5\). Combining these lower bounds with Foster’s identity and a shortest path proves the corresponding entry in (8). Its coefficient is at most \(3/2\) for \(d\ge7\), and its constant is strictly smaller than \(-33/4\).
276	
277	### Odd orders, degrees six and eight
278	
279	The proof uses a valid two-level hierarchy of cuts of sizes two and four. A newly inserted four-cut must contain **all** left ports and exclude **all** right ports. Consequently unequal-width interfaces have no shared edges, and the currents \(1/2\) and \(1/4\) are consistent.
280	
281	Even cut parity and maximality establish the internal transshipment capacity \(1/6\). Charging the interface energies to the atoms, and charging each isolated singleton atom to a neighboring nonsingleton atom, yields
282	\[
283	6R(x,y)\le n-\frac{278}{45},
284	\qquad
285	8R(x,y)\le n-\frac{278}{45}.
286	\]
287	The few dense atoms are exhaustively checked over \(\mathbb Q\). Endpoint estimates are proved separately; in degree eight they are entirely analytic. The full subset inequalities, charging margins, and exact dense-atom certificates are included in the proof and source bundle.
288	
289	### Odd orders, degrees at least ten
290	
291	Here there is a short uniform argument. In a two-connected block of order \(b\), let
292	\[
293	\Delta=\sum_v(d-\deg_Bv).
294	\]
295	A shortest cycle of length \(c\) through two specified vertices satisfies
296	\[
297	(d+1)c\le6b-10+\Delta.
298	\]
299	The reason is that its cross-chord graph has no spaced inversions and hence at most \(3(c-2)/2-2\) edges; every outside vertex has at most three neighbors on either arc.
300	
301	Averaging the resistance triangle inequalities along the two arcs and using Foster’s identity gives a local block bound. Reassembling the block path, with off-path vertices paying the off-path degree deficits, gives the last entry of (8).
302	
303	For \(d\ge10\),
304	\[
305	\frac{d^2+15d-8}{2(d+1)^2}\le1,
306	\]
307	because this is equivalent to \((d-1)(d-10)\ge0\). At \(d=10\) the subtracted constant is
308	\[
309	\frac{771}{121}>\frac{278}{45};
310	\]
311	for \(d\ge12\) it exceeds \(d/2+1\ge7\). Thus all these degrees are strictly below every odd target.
312	
313	This completes the upper-bound half for **every** admissible graph.
314	
315	## 5. Odd-order equality constructions
316	
317	The four-regular extremizers are chains of explicitly supplied modules. Their checked terminal resistances are
318	
319	\[
320	\begin{array}{c|cccc}
321	\text{cap order}&6&7&9&10\\ \hline
322	\text{root eccentricity}&
323	4/5&104/115&52/45&31/20
324	\end{array}
325	\]
326	
327	and
328	
329	\[
330	\begin{array}{c|cc}
331	\text{middle-block order}&6&8\\ \hline
332	\text{port resistance}&5/4&3/2.
333	\end{array}
334	\]
335	
336	Ports have degree two; identifying consecutive ports makes their resulting degree four. Every other vertex already has degree four. The six-vertex middle block has a \(K_4\) core, with each port joined to a disjoint pair of core vertices.
337	
338	Use the following base chains:
339	\[
340	\begin{array}{c|c}
341	n\bmod5&\text{base modules}\\ \hline
342	0&\text{cap }6,\ \text{cap }10\\
343	1&\text{cap }6,\ \text{cap }6\\
344	2&\text{cap }6,\ \text{cap }7\\
345	3&\text{cap }6,\ \text{middle }8,\ \text{cap }6\\
346	4&\text{cap }6,\ \text{cap }9.
347	\end{array}
348	\]
349	Insert enough six-vertex middle blocks to reach \(n\). Each insertion adds five vertices and resistance \(5/4\), so it preserves \(R-n/4\).
350	
351	Series resistance gives exactly the five defects in (6). The source file `odd_construction.py` supplies every edge of every module and constructs the graph for arbitrary allowed odd \(n\). It verifies simplicity, connectivity, regularity, module resistances, and full-graph resistance diameters exactly.
352	
353	Combining these constructions, the cubic constructions, (1), and all upper bounds proves
354	\[
355	\boxed{
356	\max_{G\in\mathcal R_n}\tau(G)=
357	\begin{cases}
358	\frac{3n(2n-9)}4,&n\equiv2\pmod4,\\[2pt]
359	\frac{3n(2n-11)}4,&n\equiv0\pmod4,\\[2pt]
360	n^2-\frac{28}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv0,3\pmod5,\\[2pt]
361	n^2-\frac{23}{5}n,&n\text{ odd},\ n\equiv1\pmod5,\\[2pt]
